input: Look into dual citizenship eligibility through my grandparents

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The user may have grandparents from multiple countries — knowing which specific country or countries they are targeting completely changes which laws, programs, and eligibility rules apply.

Citizenship by descent rules vary depending on whether it is a maternal or paternal grandparent, and whether the grandparent was a citizen by birth or naturalization — the specific grandparent in question determines eligibility pathways.
The user's current citizenship and country of residence affects which dual citizenship combinations are legally permitted, and may trigger specific bilateral treaties or restrictions.

The availability of key documents — birth certificates, naturalization records, marriage certificates — is often the biggest practical bottleneck and determines how far along the process can realistically go.
Some citizenship-by-descent applications have strict time limits, generational cut-offs, or require renouncing other citizenships — knowing any hard limits shapes what is actually achievable.
The user may want just a preliminary eligibility assessment, a full step-by-step action plan, or help identifying a lawyer — what 'done well' looks like determines how deep the research needs to go.
Whether the user wants to pursue this independently, hire a citizenship attorney, or use a specialist agency affects which resources and next steps are most relevant to surface.

gold.taskTitle: Research dual citizenship eligibility via grandparents
gold.taskDescription: Investigate whether the user qualifies for dual citizenship through their grandparents' nationality or descent, and determine what steps to take.

questions.title: Which country's citizenship are you trying to obtain?
questions.description: Identify the specific target country (e.g., Italy, Ireland, Poland) whose citizenship-by-descent rules will govern the entire research process.

questions.title: Which grandparent specifically — maternal, paternal, which side?
questions.description: Pinpoint the exact grandparent (e.g., maternal grandmother) since descent-line rules, generational limits, and gender-based restrictions differ significantly by country.

questions.title: What is your current citizenship or nationality?
questions.description: Establish the user's existing citizenship to check whether the target country permits dual citizenship with it, and whether any treaties or restrictions apply.

questions.title: Which key documents do you already have access to?
questions.description: Determine what records (birth certificates, naturalization papers, marriage certificates) are on hand versus still need to be sourced, as this is often the main practical bottleneck.

questions.title: Are you aware of any generational cut-offs or deadlines that apply?
questions.description: Surface any known constraints such as generational limits (e.g., only first-generation descendants qualify) or application deadlines tied to specific legal programs.

questions.title: Do you want a full action plan or just an eligibility check first?
questions.description: Clarify what the end output should look like — a quick yes/no eligibility assessment, a detailed step-by-step roadmap, or something else — so the plan is scoped appropriately.

questions.title: Do you plan to handle this yourself or hire a specialist?
questions.description: Understand whether the user wants DIY guidance and self-research resources, or recommendations for citizenship attorneys and specialist agencies to delegate to.
